topic: Ambedkar & the Making of the Constitution

items.title: Ambedkar: Life, Education & Ideas
items.body:
### Who was Ambedkar

**In one line:** Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a Dalit scholar, economist and lawyer who turned the fight against untouchability into a demand for equal rights, and later chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC pairs his life, his social movements and his constitutional role in one cluster; a single statement-based question can test his birth, his degrees and his slogan together, so the easy marks come from knowing the exact facts.

**The story**

- He was **born on 14 April 1891 at Mhow** (in present-day Madhya Pradesh) into a **Mahar** family. The Mahars were treated as 'untouchable', so as a child he faced open caste humiliation even in school.
- He studied at **Elphinstone College, Bombay**, then went abroad: an **MA and PhD in economics from Columbia University** in New York, a **D.Sc. (Doctor of Science) from the London School of Economics**, and training as a **barrister at Gray's Inn**, London.
- This made him one of the most highly educated Indian leaders of his generation. He used that learning as a weapon, combining **economics, law and social theory** to attack caste at its roots.

**Why it matters:** His argument was that caste is not a harmless 'division of labour' but a harmful **division of labourers** held in place by graded inequality. The cure, he said, is not to reform caste but to **annihilate** (completely abolish) it. His slogan — **'Educate, Agitate, Organise'** — told the oppressed to gain knowledge, demand rights and build organisations.

**Terms explained**

- **Mahar:** a Dalit (formerly 'untouchable') community of Maharashtra, Ambedkar's own community.
- **D.Sc.:** Doctor of Science, a higher research doctorate (here from the LSE).
- **Barrister:** a lawyer qualified to argue cases in the higher courts; Gray's Inn is one of London's four Inns of Court that train barristers.
- **Annihilation of caste:** destroying the caste system entirely, not merely softening it.

**Remember it:** His education trail runs **Columbia → LSE → Gray's Inn** — remember 'CLG'. His economics thesis, *The Problem of the Rupee*, later fed into the design of the **Reserve Bank of India**.

**TL;DR**

- Born 14 April 1891 at Mhow in a Mahar family.
- Degrees: PhD (Columbia), D.Sc. (LSE), Barrister (Gray's Inn).
- Slogan 'Educate, Agitate, Organise'; wanted caste abolished, not reformed.
- His thesis *The Problem of the Rupee* influenced the design of the RBI.
keyPoints: Born 14 April 1891 at Mhow in a Mahar family.
PhD (Columbia), D.Sc. (LSE), Barrister (Gray's Inn) — one of the most educated leaders of his era.
Slogan: 'Educate, Agitate, Organise'; sought caste annihilation, not reform.
His thesis The Problem of the Rupee informed the design of the Reserve Bank of India.

items.title: Ambedkar's Social Movements & Organisations
items.body:
### How Ambedkar fought untouchability

**In one line:** Through public protests (satyagrahas), journals and political parties, Ambedkar demanded civic equality and political representation for the Depressed Classes.

**Why it is asked:** Match-the-following questions love his satyagrahas, journals and parties with their years; the Communal Award versus Poona Pact contrast is a repeat favourite.

**The story**

- **Mahad Satyagraha (1927):** at Mahad he led the Depressed Classes to drink water from the public **Chavdar tank** — a basic civic right that caste rules had denied them. At a follow-up conference the **Manusmriti was publicly burned (25 December 1927)**, rejecting the old scripture that justified caste.
- **Kalaram Temple Entry (Nashik, 1930):** he demanded that the Depressed Classes be allowed into the Kalaram temple — extending the fight from water to places of worship.
- He built **journals** to shape opinion and **organisations** to mobilise people.

**Picture it — organisations & journals**

| Vehicle | Year | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Mooknayak | 1920 | First journal (aided by Shahu of Kolhapur) |
| Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha | 1924 | Welfare & education of Depressed Classes |
| Bahishkrit Bharat | 1927 | Marathi fortnightly |
| Prabuddha Bharat | 1956 | Later journal reflecting his Buddhist turn |
| Independent Labour Party | 1936 | Contested the 1937 provincial polls |
| Scheduled Castes Federation | 1942 | Political platform |
| Republican Party of India | 1956 (realised 1957) | Planned by him; formally launched after his death |

**Annihilation of Caste (1936):** this famous text was written as a **presidential speech for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal, Lahore** (a Hindu anti-caste body). The organisers found it too radical and withdrew the invitation, so the **speech was never delivered** — Ambedkar published it himself. **Don't confuse** it was not a Congress address or a memorandum to the Simon Commission.

**Constitutional advocacy:** He represented the Depressed Classes at **all three Round Table Conferences (1930–32)** in London and won **separate electorates** in the **Communal Award (1932)**. Gandhi opposed this and went on a fast-unto-death, leading to the **Poona Pact (September 1932)**: separate electorates were replaced by **reserved seats within a joint electorate** (seats raised from 71 to 148 in the provinces).

**Terms explained**

- **Satyagraha:** a non-violent protest or civil-disobedience campaign.
- **Depressed Classes:** the colonial-era term for the castes later called Scheduled Castes/Dalits.
- **Separate electorate:** only voters of one community vote for, and elect, candidates of that community.
- **Joint electorate with reserved seats:** everyone votes together, but some seats are set aside only for a particular community's candidates.

**Don't confuse:** **Mahad (1927) = water** at the Chavdar tank; **Kalaram, Nashik (1930) = temple entry**. **Communal Award = separate electorates**; **Poona Pact = reserved seats** that replaced them.

**Remember it:** Communal Award (1932) gave the gift of a separate electorate; the Poona Pact of the same year took it back and gave reserved seats instead.

**TL;DR**

- Mahad Satyagraha (1927): Chavdar tank water rights + burning of the Manusmriti.
- Kalaram Temple Entry launched at Nashik in 1930.
- Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) were early tools.
- Communal Award (1932) gave separate electorates; Poona Pact replaced them with reserved seats.
- Parties: Independent Labour Party (1936) -> Scheduled Castes Federation (1942) -> RPI (1956/57).
keyPoints: Mahad Satyagraha (1927): Chavdar tank water rights + burning of the Manusmriti.

items.title: Constituent Assembly: Demand, Formation & Composition
items.body:
### How the Constituent Assembly came to be

**In one line:** The Constituent Assembly was the elected body of Indians that wrote the Constitution; the idea took over a decade to go from a proposal to a real, working assembly in 1946.

**Why it is asked:** The chain of events (idea -> demand -> plan -> assembly) and the exact seat numbers are classic statement-based and match questions.

**The story**

- **1934:** the idea of a Constituent Assembly is first put forward by **M.N. Roy**.
- **1935:** the **Indian National Congress (INC)** formally demands one; **1938:** Nehru insists it must be made up of elected Indians.
- **1940:** the British concede the idea in principle (the **August Offer**); **1942:** the **Cripps Mission** promises it after the Second World War.
- **1946:** it is finally set up under the **Cabinet Mission Plan**; elections are held in **July 1946**; the first meeting is on **9 December 1946**.

**Picture it — planned composition**

| Category | Seats |
|---|---|
| British provinces | 292 |
| Chief commissioners' provinces | 4 |
| Princely states | 93 |
| Total | 389 |
| After partition | 299 |

**Why it matters:** Because members were **indirectly elected** by the provincial assemblies (using proportional representation with a single transferable vote, roughly 1 seat for every 10 lakh people), the Assembly was not chosen by the whole adult public — a point exams test as a 'trap'. Princely-state seats were filled by the rulers' nominees.

**Terms explained**

- **Constituent Assembly:** a body specially elected to frame (write) a constitution.
- **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946):** a British proposal that set up the Assembly and a scheme for grouping provinces.
- **Indirect election:** the public elects legislators, who in turn elect the Assembly members (so the public does not vote for them directly).
- **Single transferable vote (STV):** a proportional system where voters rank candidates and surplus votes transfer to later preferences.

**Don't confuse:** the Assembly was set up under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**, not the Cripps Mission (1942) — Cripps only promised it. Members were **indirectly elected**, NOT elected by universal adult franchise.

**Remember it:** '3-8-9' — the planned strength was **389**; after partition it fell to **299** (drop the first digit's extra and swap).

**TL;DR**

- Idea first proposed by M.N. Roy (1934); INC demanded it in 1935.
- Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946; elections July 1946; first meeting 9 Dec 1946.
- Planned strength 389 seats (292 + 4 + 93 princely states); reduced to 299 after partition.
- Members indirectly elected by proportional representation with a single transferable vote.
keyPoints: Idea first proposed by M.N. Roy (1934); INC demanded it in 1935.
Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946; elections July 1946; first meeting 9 Dec 1946.

items.title: Office-bearers & the Objectives Resolution
items.body:
### Who ran the Assembly, and its founding vision

**In one line:** When the Assembly first met it elected its presiding officers, and Nehru's Objectives Resolution set out the ideals that later became the Preamble.

**Why it is asked:** The office-bearers are a standard match-the-following set, and the Objectives Resolution's mover and dates are frequently tested.

**The story**

- At the first sitting on **9 December 1946**, **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha** presided as the temporary (provisional) President because he was the **oldest member** — a borrowed convention.
- On **11 December 1946** the Assembly elected **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** as its permanent President.
- **Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946**; it was **adopted on 22 January 1947**. It declared India an **independent sovereign republic** and promised justice, equality and liberty, with safeguards for minorities and depressed classes. Its ideals were carried almost word-for-word into the **Preamble**.

**Picture it — presiding officers**

| Role | Person | Date |
|---|---|---|
| First (provisional) President | Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha | 9 Dec 1946 |
| Permanent President | Dr. Rajendra Prasad | 11 Dec 1946 |
| Vice-President | H.C. Mukherjee | — |
| Constitutional Advisor | Sir B.N. Rau | — |

**Terms explained**

- **Provisional President:** a temporary chairperson until a permanent one is elected.
- **Constitutional Advisor:** the official (B.N. Rau) who prepared the initial working draft for the Assembly to debate; he advised but was not an elected member.
- **Objectives Resolution:** Nehru's resolution stating the aims and philosophy of the Constitution.
- **Preamble:** the opening declaration of the Constitution stating its ideals.

**Don't confuse:** **Sinha** was only the first/provisional President; the **permanent** President was **Rajendra Prasad**. **B.N. Rau** (Constitutional Advisor) is not the same as the Drafting Committee chairman (Ambedkar).

**Remember it:** the Objectives Resolution was **moved on 13 Dec 1946** and **passed on 22 Jan 1947** — moved before Christmas, passed before Republic month.

**TL;DR**

- Provisional President Sachchidananda Sinha; permanent President Rajendra Prasad (11 Dec 1946).
- H.C. Mukherjee was Vice-President; B.N. Rau the Constitutional Advisor.
- Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, passed on 22 Jan 1947.
- The Objectives Resolution became the philosophical basis of the Preamble.
keyPoints: Provisional President Sachchidananda Sinha; permanent President Rajendra Prasad (11 Dec 1946).
H.C. Mukherjee was Vice-President; B.N. Rau the Constitutional Advisor.
Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, passed on 22 Jan 1947.
The Objectives Resolution became the philosophical basis of the Preamble.

items.title: Committees & the Drafting Committee
items.body:
### The committees that built the Constitution

**In one line:** The Assembly divided its work among many committees; the most famous, the Drafting Committee under Ambedkar, turned the proposals into the final text.

**Why it is asked:** The committee-to-chairman match and the membership of the Drafting Committee (including who was NOT on it) are repeat questions.

**The story**

- The Assembly worked through **8 major and several minor committees** and held **11 sessions**. Big names chaired the big committees.
- The **Drafting Committee** was constituted on **29 August 1947** with **seven members** and was chaired by **Ambedkar**, who steered the draft through clause-by-clause debate.

**Picture it — major committees & chairmen**

| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Union Powers / Union Constitution / States (negotiating with princely states) | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| Provincial Constitution / Advisory (Fundamental Rights, Minorities, Tribal Areas) | Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel |
| Drafting Committee | Dr. B.R. Ambedkar |
| Rules of Procedure | Dr. Rajendra Prasad |

**The seven Drafting Committee members:**

1. **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (Chairman)**
2. K.M. Munshi
3. **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** (Telugu jurist, Madras Presidency)
4. N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar
5. Syed Mohammad Saadulla
6. N. Madhava Rau (replaced B.L. Mitter)
7. T.T. Krishnamachari (replaced D.P. Khaitan)

**Why it matters:** Ambedkar's command of the text earned him the title **'Father of the Indian Constitution'**. Note that **Sardar Patel was NOT on the Drafting Committee** — he chaired the Provincial Constitution and Advisory committees (the States Committee was Nehru's), which is a common exam trap.

**Terms explained**

- **Drafting Committee:** the committee that prepared and refined the actual wording of the Constitution.
- **Jurist:** an expert in law; Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was a leading one from the Telugu region.

**Don't confuse:** **Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting** Committee; **Nehru** the **Union** and **States** committees; **Patel** the **Provincial/Advisory** committees; **Rajendra Prasad** the **Rules** committee.

**Remember it:** two members replaced two others — **Madhava Rau in for B.L. Mitter**, **T.T. Krishnamachari in for D.P. Khaitan**.

**TL;DR**

- Union and States committees chaired by Nehru; Provincial/Advisory by Patel; Drafting by Ambedkar; Rules by Rajendra Prasad.
- Drafting Committee set up 29 August 1947 with seven members.
- Members included K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Saadulla, Madhava Rau, T.T. Krishnamachari.
- Ambedkar's stewardship earned him the title 'Father of the Indian Constitution'.
keyPoints: Union and States committees chaired by Nehru; Provincial/Advisory by Patel; Drafting by Ambedkar; Rules by Rajendra Prasad.

items.title: Timeline, Andhra Members & Legacy
items.body:
### Key dates, Telugu members and Ambedkar's later life

**In one line:** The Constitution was adopted in 1949 and came into force in 1950; several Telugu leaders helped frame it, and Ambedkar's later life ended with his conversion to Buddhism.

**Why it is asked:** The two 'adopted vs in force' dates are the single most common prelims trap; the Andhra members give the natural AP angle; the legacy facts round out the cluster.

**Picture it — making of the Constitution**

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 9 Dec 1946 | First meeting (Sinha presiding) |
| 13 Dec 1946 | Objectives Resolution moved |
| 22 Jan 1947 | Objectives Resolution adopted |
| 29 Aug 1947 | Drafting Committee formed |
| 26 Nov 1949 | Constitution adopted/enacted |
| 26 Jan 1950 | Constitution came into force |

**The story:** Framing took about **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**. The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (now Constitution Day) but **came into force on 26 January 1950**, a date chosen to honour the 1930 Purna Swaraj (complete independence) pledge.

**Andhra members of the Assembly:** **Durgabai Deshmukh** (founder of the Andhra Mahila Sabha), **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** (Drafting Committee), **N.G. Ranga**, **Pattabhi Sitaramayya**, **Tanguturi Prakasam** ('Andhra Kesari'), **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** and **Moturi Satyanarayana**.

**Ambedkar's later career:** he became independent India's **first Law Minister**, then **resigned in 1951**, partly over the stalling of the **Hindu Code Bill** (a reform of Hindu personal law). He **embraced Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 October 1956** with lakhs of followers, and **died on 6 December 1956**. He founded the **Republican Party of India** and was awarded the **Bharat Ratna (1990)** after his death.

**Terms explained**

- **Adopted/enacted:** the day the Assembly formally approved the Constitution (26 Nov 1949).
- **Came into force / commenced:** the day it legally took effect (26 Jan 1950).
- **Hindu Code Bill:** a set of laws to reform Hindu marriage, succession and women's rights.
- **Bharat Ratna:** India's highest civilian award.

**Don't confuse:** **26 Nov 1949 = adopted**; **26 Jan 1950 = in force**. Independence (15 Aug 1947) is a third, separate date.

**Remember it:** 'Adopted in '49, alive in '50' — written down first, switched on later.

**TL;DR**

- Adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; took about 2 years 11 months 18 days.
- Andhra members: Durgabai Deshmukh, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N.G. Ranga, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, T. Prakasam.
- Ambedkar was first Law Minister; resigned 1951 over the Hindu Code Bill.
- Converted to Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 Oct 1956; died 6 Dec 1956; Bharat Ratna 1990.
keyPoints: Adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; took about 2 years 11 months 18 days.

items.title: Other Members, Symbols & Framing Facts (PYQ set)
items.body:
### The facts examiners quietly test

**In one line:** Beyond the famous names, exams test a handful of other Assembly members, the dates the national symbols were adopted, and small 'framing facts' such as the cost and the calligrapher.

**Why it is asked:** These are precise, one-fact questions (who chaired the First Finance Commission, when the flag was adopted) that are easy marks if memorised and easy to miss if not.

**The story — other notable members**

- **K.C. Neogy** — an Assembly member who later chaired the **First Finance Commission (1951)**.
- Members often paired in exams: **H.C. Mukherjee** (Vice-President), **G.V. Mavalankar** (Speaker of the legislative wing), **Frank Anthony** (represented Anglo-Indians), **H.P. Modi** (Parsis) and **Begum Aizaz Rasul**.

**Picture it — national symbols adopted by the Assembly**

| Symbol | Adopted on |
|---|---|
| National Flag | 22 July 1947 |
| National Anthem ('Jana Gana Mana') & National Song ('Vande Mataram') | 24 January 1950 |
| State Emblem (Lion Capital of Sarnath) | 26 January 1950 |

**Framing facts & figures:**

- The Assembly held **11 sessions** over **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**; members signed the Constitution on **24 January 1950**.
- Total expenditure was about **₹64 lakh**.
- **Prem Behari Narain Raizada** hand-wrote (calligraphed) the original Constitution; **Nandalal Bose** and his team illustrated it.
- The Assembly also served as the **provisional Parliament** (1950–52) until the first general elections.

**Terms explained**

- **Finance Commission:** a body that recommends how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the states; the first was set up in 1951.
- **Calligraphed:** written by hand in an ornamental script.
- **Provisional Parliament:** a temporary legislature that functioned until the first elected Parliament.

**Don't confuse:** the **Flag was adopted 22 July 1947** (before independence); the **Anthem and Song on 24 January 1950** (just before Republic Day). Do not mix these with 26 Nov 1949 or 26 Jan 1950.

**Remember it:** 'Flag before freedom (22 Jul 1947); songs before Republic Day (24 Jan 1950).'

**TL;DR**

- K.C. Neogy was a Constituent Assembly member and chaired the First Finance Commission (1951).
- National Flag adopted 22 July 1947; National Anthem & Song adopted 24 January 1950.
- Signed on 24 Jan 1950; framing took 2 years 11 months 18 days over 11 sessions.
- Cost about ₹64 lakh; hand-calligraphed by Prem Behari Narain Raizada, illustrated by Nandalal Bose.
- The Assembly acted as the provisional Parliament until the 1951–52 elections.
keyPoints: K.C. Neogy was a Constituent Assembly member and chaired the First Finance Commission (1951).

items.title: Ambedkar's Public Career, 1913–1956 — Detail
items.body:
### Ambedkar's Public Career, 1913–1956 — Detail

**In one line**
The milestones between the scholarship that sent him abroad and the memorials that honour him today.

**The story**
Ambedkar's father **Ramji Maloji Sakpal** was an army subedar; the family hailed from **Ambadawe** in Ratnagiri. A scholarship from **Sayajirao Gaekwad** III of Baroda sent him to Columbia, where his PhD thesis was on the **Evolution of Provincial Finance** in British India. Back home he pressed the Depressed Classes' case before every British body: the **Southborough** Committee (1919), the **Bombay Legislative Council** (nominated 1926) and, as a member of the **Bombay Presidency Committee**, the Simon Commission (1928). At **Yeola** in 1935 he announced he would not die a Hindu. In 1942–46 he was **Labour Member** of the Viceroy's Executive Council. He entered the Constituent Assembly from Bengal with **Jogendra Nath Mandal**'s help, and after partition returned through the Bombay seat of M.R. **Jayakar**. He quit the cabinet in **September 1951**, lost the 1952 poll to N.S. **Kajrolkar**, and built colleges through the **People's Education Society** (Siddharth, **Milind College**). At Nagpur Bhadant U **Chandramani** initiated him into Buddhism and he gave the **22 vows**; he was cremated at **Chaitya Bhoomi**, and the five memorial sites are called the **Panchteerth**.

#### Career milestones

| Milestone | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Father** | **Ramji Maloji Sakpal**, army subedar at Mhow |
| **Ancestral village** | **Ambadawe**, Ratnagiri (surname from Ambadawekar) |
| **Patron** | **Sayajirao Gaekwad** III of Baroda — scholarship to Columbia (1913) |
| **Columbia degrees** | MA 1915; PhD thesis **Evolution of Provincial Finance** in British India (pub. 1925) |
| **1919** | Evidence to the **Southborough** (Franchise) Committee — separate electorates |
| **1926** | Nominated to the **Bombay Legislative Council** |
| **1928** | Simon Commission — member, **Bombay Presidency Committee** |
| **Yeola, 1935** | 'Born a Hindu, but I will not die a Hindu' (13 Oct 1935) |
| **1942–46** | **Labour Member**, Viceroy's Executive Council |
| **Entry to the Assembly** | Elected from Bengal with **Jogendra Nath Mandal**'s support (1946) |
| **Seat after partition** | Bombay seat vacated by M.R. **Jayakar** (1947) |
| **Resignation** | **September 1951** — Hindu Code Bill stalled |
| **1952 election** | Lost Bombay North to N.S. **Kajrolkar**; went to the Rajya Sabha |
| **Education work** | **People's Education Society** (1945) — Siddharth College (1946), **Milind College**, Aurangabad (1950) |
| **Deeksha, Nagpur** | Initiated by Bhadant U **Chandramani**; Ambedkar gave the **22 vows** |
| **Death & memorial** | 26 Alipur Road, Delhi; cremated at **Chaitya Bhoomi**, Dadar; 6 Dec = **Mahaparinirvan** Diwas |
| **Panchteerth** | Mhow · London (10 King Henry's Road) · Nagpur · Delhi · Mumbai |

**Don't confuse**
- **Southborough Committee (1919)** = franchise; **Simon Commission (1928)** = constitutional review. Both heard Ambedkar.
- **Labour Member (1942–46)** of the Viceroy's Council ≠ **Law Minister (1947–51)** of independent India.

**TL;DR**
- Father Ramji Maloji Sakpal; Gaekwad scholarship; PhD thesis on provincial finance.
- Southborough 1919; Bombay Council 1926; Simon Commission 1928; Yeola 1935.
- Labour Member 1942–46; CA seat from Bengal (J.N. Mandal), then Bombay (Jayakar); resigned September 1951.
- Chandramani & 22 vows (Nagpur 1956); Chaitya Bhoomi; Panchteerth.
keyPoints: Ambedkar testified before the Southborough Committee in 1919.
At Yeola (1935) Ambedkar declared he would not die a Hindu.
Ambedkar was Labour Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council, 1942–46.
Jogendra Nath Mandal helped Ambedkar win a Constituent Assembly seat from Bengal.

items.title: Ambedkar's Books and Journals — Detail
items.body:
### Ambedkar's Books and Journals — Detail

**In one line**
A scholar who wrote across economics, history, religion and constitutional law — and the journals through which he spoke to his people.

**The story**
Ambedkar's first scholarly paper, ***Castes in India*** (**1916**), argued that endogamy is the essence of caste. His economics produced ***The Problem of the Rupee*** (**1923**), and his currency evidence reached the **Hilton Young** Commission. In the 1940s he wrote on politics and history: ***Thoughts on Pakistan*** (1940), *Ranade, Gandhi and Jinnah* (1943), the polemic ***What Congress and Gandhi Have Done*** to the Untouchables (1945), ***Who Were the Shudras*** (1946), the Assembly memorandum ***States and Minorities*** (1947) and ***The Untouchables*** (**1948**). ***Thoughts on Linguistic States*** came in **1955**, and ***The Buddha and His Dhamma*** was published after his death (**1957**). His journals were *Mooknayak* — '**Leader of the Voiceless**' — *Bahishkrit Bharat*, ***Samata*** (**1928**) and ***Janata*** (**1930**). The first Dalit journal, *Vital Vidhvansak* (1888), was Gopal Baba **Walangkar**'s. Since **2015** his legacy is honoured every 26 November as **Samvidhan Divas**.

#### Books

| Book | Year / note |
|---|---|
| *Castes in India* | **1916** — Columbia seminar paper |
| *The Problem of the Rupee* | **1923** — LSE D.Sc. thesis; fed the Hilton Young Commission |
| Hilton Young link | **Hilton Young** Commission 1926 → RBI 1935 |
| *Thoughts on Pakistan* | 1940 (later *Pakistan or the Partition of India*) |
| *Ranade, Gandhi and Jinnah* | 1943 lecture |
| *What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables* | 1945 |
| *Who Were the Shudras?* | 1946 — origin of the Shudras |
| *States and Minorities* | 1947 — memorandum to the Assembly (SC Federation) |
| *The Untouchables* | **1948** |
| *Thoughts on Linguistic States* | **1955** — written as the SRC reported |
| *The Buddha and His Dhamma* | **1957** — posthumous |

#### Journals and days

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| *Mooknayak* — meaning | '**Leader of the Voiceless**' (31 Jan 1920) |
| *Samata* | **1928** — organ of the Samaj Samata Sangh |
| *Janata* | **1930** → renamed *Prabuddha Bharat* (1956) |
| *Vital Vidhvansak* (trap) | 1888 — Gopal Baba **Walangkar**, not Ambedkar |
| **Constitution Day** | 26 Nov — **Samvidhan Divas** since **2015** (earlier Law Day) |

**Don't confuse**
- ***Vital Vidhvansak*** (Walangkar, 1888) is a favourite distractor — Ambedkar's journals are Mooknayak, Bahishkrit Bharat, Samata, Janata.
- ***Annihilation of Caste*** (1936, undelivered speech) ≠ ***Castes in India*** (1916, Columbia paper).

**TL;DR**
- Castes in India 1916; Problem of the Rupee 1923; Thoughts on Pakistan 1940.
- What Congress and Gandhi Have Done… 1945; Who Were the Shudras? 1946; The Untouchables 1948.
- Thoughts on Linguistic States 1955; The Buddha and His Dhamma 1957 (posthumous).
- Journals: Mooknayak 1920, Bahishkrit Bharat 1927, Samata 1928, Janata 1930; Samvidhan Divas since 2015.
keyPoints: Ambedkar's D.Sc. thesis was The Problem of the Rupee (1923).
Who Were the Shudras? appeared in 1946.
The Buddha and His Dhamma was published posthumously in 1957.

items.title: Satyagrahas, Round Tables and the Poona Pact — Detail
items.body:
### Satyagrahas, Round Tables and the Poona Pact — Detail

**In one line**
The dates and names behind Ambedkar's campaigns, and the 1932 bargain that changed Depressed-Class representation.

**The story**
The **Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha** (Bombay, **20 July 1924**) — which the source PDF calls the **Depressed Classes Institute** — organised the first protests. On **20 March 1927** Ambedkar marched to the Chavdar tank at Mahad; on **25 December 1927** the Manusmriti was burnt. Temple entry followed: **Parvati** (Pune, 1929) and Kalaram, Nashik (**2 March 1930**). At the First Round Table Conference Ambedkar and R. **Srinivasan** spoke for the Depressed Classes. Their demand was granted in **Ramsay MacDonald**'s Communal Award (**16 August 1932**). Gandhi, in **Yerawada** jail, fasted against it. The **Poona Pact** of **24 September 1932**, signed by Ambedkar and Madan Mohan **Malaviya**, replaced separate electorates with reserved seats (71 → 148 in the provinces, **18 per cent** at the Centre). Gandhi then founded the **Anti-Untouchability League**. Ambedkar's later Scheduled Castes Federation was founded at **Nagpur** in **July 1942**.

#### Campaign dates and names

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha** | Bombay, **20 July 1924** |
| **Depressed Classes Institute** | 1924 (source PDF name for the same Sabha) |
| **Mahad march** | Chavdar tank, **20 March 1927** |
| **Manusmriti burnt** | **25 December 1927** — Manusmriti Dahan Din |
| **Parvati temple** | Pune, 1929 — temple-entry satyagraha |
| **Kalaram, Nashik** | Began **2 March 1930** |
| **First RTC (1930)** | Depressed Classes: Ambedkar & R. **Srinivasan** |
| **Communal Award** | **Ramsay MacDonald**, **16 August 1932** |
| **Gandhi's fast** | **Yerawada** jail, from 20 Sept 1932 |
| **Poona Pact** | Signed **24 September 1932** |
| **Signatories** | Ambedkar (Depressed Classes) & Madan Mohan **Malaviya** (caste Hindus) |
| **Central seats** | **18 per cent** of general seats in the central legislature |
| **Gandhi's response** | All-India **Anti-Untouchability League** (1932) → Harijan Sevak Sangh; *Harijan* 1933 |
| **SC Federation** | Founded at **Nagpur**, **July 1942** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Communal Award** (MacDonald, 16 Aug 1932) → **fast** (Yerawada, 20 Sept) → **Poona Pact** (24 Sept 1932). Award = separate electorates; Pact = reserved seats.
- **Malaviya** signed for caste Hindus — not Nehru or Patel.

**TL;DR**
- BHS 20 July 1924; Mahad 20 March 1927; Manusmriti burnt 25 Dec 1927.
- Parvati (Pune) 1929; Kalaram (Nashik) 2 March 1930.
- RTC-I: Ambedkar & R. Srinivasan; Communal Award 16 Aug 1932 (MacDonald).
- Yerawada fast → Poona Pact 24 Sept 1932 (Malaviya); 18% central seats; SCF Nagpur 1942.
keyPoints: The Communal Award was announced by Ramsay MacDonald on 16 August 1932.
The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932.
Madan Mohan Malaviya signed the Poona Pact for the caste Hindus.
The Manusmriti was burnt on 25 December 1927 at Mahad.

items.title: Every Committee of the Constituent Assembly and its Chairman
items.body:
### Every Committee of the Constituent Assembly and its Chairman

**In one line**
Eight major committees, a dozen minor ones and four sub-committees — the full chairman list that match questions draw from.

**The story**
The Assembly worked through **8 major** committees and about **15 minor** committees. **Nehru** chaired the **Union Powers Committee**, the **Union Constitution Committee**, the **States Committee** and the **Special Committee** that examined the Draft. **Patel** chaired the **Provincial Constitution Committee** and the **Advisory Committee**. **Rajendra Prasad** chaired the Rules of Procedure, **Steering Committee**, **Finance and Staff Committee** and the **Ad-hoc Committee on the National Flag**. Under Patel's Advisory Committee sat sub-committees: Fundamental Rights (**Kripalani**), the **Minorities Sub-Committee** (H.C. Mukherjee), the North-East tribal areas (**Bardoloi**) and other excluded areas (**Thakkar**). Two Telugu leaders chaired committees: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar the **Credentials Committee**, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya the **House Committee** and the Committee on **Chief Commissioners' Provinces**. Others: **Order of Business** (Munshi), **Functions of the Constituent Assembly** (Mavalankar), Supreme Court (**Varadachari**), financial provisions (**Nalini Ranjan Ghosh**) and the press gallery (**Usha Nath Sen**). The Drafting Committee's seven were Ambedkar, Alladi, **K.M. Munshi** (founder of the **Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan**), **Gopalaswamy Ayyangar** (ex-Dewan of **Jammu and Kashmir**), **Saadulla** (ex-Premier of **Assam**), **Madhava Rau** (for **B.L. Mitter**) and **T.T. Krishnamachari** (for D.P. **Khaitan**).

#### Committees and chairmen

| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| **Union Powers Committee** | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| **Union Constitution Committee** | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| **States Committee** (negotiating with States) | Jawaharlal Nehru — not Patel |
| **Special Committee** to examine the Draft | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| **Provincial Constitution Committee** | Sardar Patel |
| **Advisory Committee** (FR, Minorities, Tribal & Excluded Areas) | Sardar Patel |
| **Steering Committee** | Rajendra Prasad |
| **Finance and Staff Committee** | Rajendra Prasad |
| **Ad-hoc Committee on the National Flag** | Rajendra Prasad |
| **Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee** | J.B. Kripalani |
| **Minorities Sub-Committee** | H.C. Mukherjee |
| **North-East Frontier Tribal Areas & Assam Sub-Committee** | Gopinath Bardoloi |
| **Excluded Areas (other than Assam) Sub-Committee** | A.V. Thakkar |
| **Credentials Committee** | Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar |
| **House Committee** | B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya |
| **Committee on Chief Commissioners' Provinces** | B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya |
| **Order of Business Committee** | K.M. Munshi |
| **Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly** | G.V. Mavalankar |
| **Ad-hoc Committee on the Supreme Court** | S. Varadachari |
| **Expert Committee on Financial Provisions** | Nalini Ranjan Ghosh |
| **Press Gallery Committee** | Usha Nath Sen |

#### Drafting Committee members

| Role | Member |
|---|---|
| Member | **K.M. Munshi** — founder of the **Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan** |
| Member | **N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar** — former Dewan of **Jammu and Kashmir** |
| Member | **Syed Mohammad Saadulla** — former Premier of **Assam** |
| Replacement | **N. Madhava Rau** in for **B.L. Mitter** |
| Replacement | **T.T. Krishnamachari** in for **D.P. Khaitan** (d. 1948) |

**Don't confuse**
- **States Committee = Nehru**; **Provincial Constitution & Advisory = Patel**. The most repeated trap.
- **T.T. Krishnamachari** (Drafting Committee) ≠ **V.T. Krishnamachari** (Vice-President of the Assembly).
- Nehru, Patel and Rajendra Prasad were **not** on the Drafting Committee.

**TL;DR**
- Nehru: Union Powers, Union Constitution, States, Special Committee on the Draft.
- Patel: Provincial Constitution, Advisory (FR, minorities, tribal areas).
- Prasad: Rules, Steering, Finance & Staff, National Flag. Sub-committees: Kripalani (FR), H.C. Mukherjee (minorities), Bardoloi, Thakkar.
- Alladi: Credentials; Pattabhi: House & Chief Commissioners' Provinces; Munshi: Order of Business; Mavalankar: Functions.
keyPoints: The States Committee of the Constituent Assembly was chaired by Nehru.
The Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee was chaired by J.B. Kripalani.
Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar chaired the Credentials Committee.
T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan on the Drafting Committee.

items.title: From First Sitting to Final Text — Numbers, Readings and Speeches
items.body:
### From First Sitting to Final Text — Numbers, Readings and Speeches

**In one line**
How the Assembly was made up, how the draft moved through three readings, and what Ambedkar warned at the end.

**The story**
In July 1946 the Congress won **208** seats and the Muslim League **73**. Provincial members were chosen by the **Provincial Legislative Assemblies**. The League **boycotted** the Assembly, so **211** members attended the first sitting. Sinha presided under the **French** practice of seniority. The Vice-Presidents were H.C. Mukherjee and **V.T. Krishnamachari**. Six princely States took seats on **28 April 1947**. B.N. Rau's first draft came in **October 1947**, and the Draft Constitution was published in **February 1948**. Ambedkar moved it on **4 November 1948**. **7,635** amendments were proposed and **2,473** discussed. The second reading ended on **17 October 1949** and the third began on **14 November 1949**. In all the Assembly sat **165 days**, **114 days** of them on the Draft. The text of **395** Articles, **22 Parts** and **8 Schedules** was passed on 26 November 1949. **Citizenship**, **elections** and transitional articles took effect that same day. **284** members signed on 24 January 1950 and elected Rajendra Prasad **first President of India**. Vasant Krishan Vaidya wrote the Hindi copy; Beohar Rammanohar Sinha decorated the Preamble page. The Assembly's seal was the **elephant**. It ratified **Commonwealth** membership in **May 1949**. Women members included **Dakshayani Velayudhan** and **Hansa Mehta**. **Granville Austin** called the Constitution the cornerstone of a nation. On 25 November 1949 Ambedkar warned against the '**grammar of anarchy**' and **hero-worship**, and against a '**life of contradictions**'. Elsewhere he called **Article 32** the **heart** and soul of the Constitution, and the Directive Principles a '**novel feature**'. He said **constitutional morality** must be cultivated.

#### Making the text

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **1946 result** | Congress **208**, Muslim League **73**, others 15 |
| **First sitting** | Muslim League **boycotted**; **211** members attended |
| **Mode of election** | Provincial members elected by the **Provincial Legislative Assemblies** (STV) |
| **Vice-Presidents** | H.C. Mukherjee & **V.T. Krishnamachari** |
| **Why Sinha** | Oldest member — **French** practice |
| **Princes join** | Six States took seats **28 April 1947** |
| **First draft** | B.N. Rau, **October 1947** |
| **Draft published** | **February 1948** |
| **Amendments** | **7,635** proposed; **2,473** discussed |
| **First reading** | **4 November 1948** — Ambedkar moves the draft |
| **Second reading** | 15 Nov 1948 – **17 October 1949** |
| **Third reading** | **14 November 1949** → passed 26 Nov 1949 |
| **Sittings** | **165 days** in all; **114 days** on the Draft |
| **Original text** | Preamble + **395** Articles, **22 Parts**, **8 Schedules** |
| **In force 26 Nov 1949** | **citizenship**, **elections**, provisional Parliament, transitional articles |
| **Signatories** | **284** members, 24 Jan 1950 |
| **24 Jan 1950** | Rajendra Prasad elected **first President of India** |
| **Artwork** | Hindi text: **Vasant Krishan Vaidya**; Preamble page: **Beohar Rammanohar Sinha** |
| **Seal** | The **elephant** |
| **Commonwealth** | Ratified **May 1949** |
| **Women members** | About 15 — **Dakshayani Velayudhan** (only Dalit woman), Begum Aizaz Rasul (only Muslim woman) |
| **Flag presented** | **Hansa Mehta**, for India's women, 14 Aug 1947 |
| **Verdict** | **Granville Austin** — "Cornerstone of a Nation"; "the Assembly was the Congress…" |

#### Ambedkar's words

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Warning 1** | Give up the '**grammar of anarchy**' (satyagraha, civil disobedience) |
| **Warning 2** | No **hero-worship** / bhakti in politics |
| **Warning 3** | 'A **life of contradictions**' — political democracy must become social democracy |
| **Article 32** | 'The very soul … and the very **heart** of it' |
| **Directive Principles** | A '**novel feature**' |
| **Constitutional morality** | Not natural — must be **cultivated** (after Grote) |

**Don't confuse**
- **26 Nov 1949**: adopted + citizenship/election articles in force; **26 Jan 1950**: the rest in force; **24 Jan 1950**: signed, President elected, anthem adopted.
- **V.T. Krishnamachari** = Vice-President; **T.T. Krishnamachari** = Drafting Committee.

**TL;DR**
- 1946: Congress 208, League 73; League boycott; 211 at first sitting; provincial members elected by provincial assemblies.
- Rau draft Oct 1947; Draft published Feb 1948; first reading 4 Nov 1948; 7,635 / 2,473 amendments; 165 days, 114 on the Draft.
- 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules; citizenship/elections in force 26 Nov 1949; 284 signatures and first President on 24 Jan 1950.
- 25 Nov 1949: 'grammar of anarchy', hero-worship, 'life of contradictions'; Article 32 'heart and soul'; DPSP 'novel feature'.

**Ambedkar’s phrases — what each referred to**
- **“Grammar of anarchy”** — using **unconstitutional methods** (satyagraha, civil disobedience) once constitutional ones are available.
- **“A life of contradictions”** — **political equality alongside social and economic inequality**.
- He called the **Directive Principles of State Policy** **“a novel feature”** of the Constitution.
keyPoints: Provincial members of the Constituent Assembly were elected by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies.
The original Constitution had 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.
Citizenship and election provisions came into force on 26 November 1949.
Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution.
Ambedkar warned against the 'grammar of anarchy' on 25 November 1949.

Ambedkar’s “grammar of anarchy” = unconstitutional methods once constitutional ones exist; “life of contradictions” = political equality with social and economic inequality; the DPSP = “a novel feature”.

items.title: Andhra in the Assembly, and Ambedkar in Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
### Andhra in the Assembly, and Ambedkar in Andhra Pradesh

**In one line**
Telugu members shaped the Assembly's committees and debates; Ambedkar, in turn, is remembered in AP's capital region and in a district name.

**The story**
Besides Prakasam, Ranga, Pattabhi and Sanjeeva Reddy, three Telugu members stand out. **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar**, born at **Pudur** in Nellore and **Advocate-General** of Madras, sat on the Drafting Committee. **Durgabai Deshmukh** of Rajahmundry was the only woman on the **Panel of Chairmen**; she later headed the **Central Social Welfare Board**. **M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar** of Tirupati later became Speaker of the Lok Sabha. **Moturi Satyanarayana**, of the Dakshina Bharat **Hindi Prachar Sabha**, spoke in the language debate. The flag the Assembly adopted grew from **Pingali Venkayya**'s design. Ambedkar's 1955 book proposed Hyderabad as India's **second capital**. Today a 125-ft **Statue of Social Justice** stands at Swaraj Maidan, **Vijayawada** (2024). **Konaseema** district (HQ **Amalapuram**) was renamed after him in 2022.

#### Andhra links

| Person / place | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** | Born **Pudur**, Nellore; **Advocate-General** of Madras 1929–44; Drafting & Credentials |
| **Durgabai Deshmukh** | Only woman on the **Panel of Chairmen**; born Rajahmundry |
| **Durgabai — later** | First chair, **Central Social Welfare Board** (1953) |
| **M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar** | Tirupati; later Lok Sabha Speaker (1956–62), Governor of Bihar |
| **Moturi Satyanarayana** | Dakshina Bharat **Hindi Prachar Sabha**; official-language debate |
| **National Flag** | Based on **Pingali Venkayya**'s design (adopted 22 July 1947) |
| **Hyderabad** | Ambedkar (1955): make it India's **second capital** |
| **Statue of Social Justice** | 125 ft, Swaraj Maidan, **Vijayawada** — unveiled 19 Jan 2024 |
| **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema** | District renamed 2022; HQ **Amalapuram** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Statue of Social Justice** (125 ft) is at **Vijayawada**, AP (Jan 2024); Telangana's 125-ft Ambedkar statue is at **Hyderabad** (Apr 2023). The **Statue of Unity** (Patel) is in Gujarat.
- **Durgabai** founded the Andhra Mahila Sabha (1937) and headed the Central Social Welfare Board (1953).

**TL;DR**
- Alladi: Pudur (Nellore), Advocate-General of Madras, Drafting & Credentials committees.
- Durgabai: only woman on the Panel of Chairmen; first chair of the CSWB (1953).
- Ananthasayanam Ayyangar (Tirupati) → Lok Sabha Speaker; Moturi Satyanarayana → Hindi Prachar Sabha.
- Ambedkar & AP: Hyderabad as second capital (1955); Statue of Social Justice, Vijayawada (2024); Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema (2022).
keyPoints: Durgabai Deshmukh was the only woman on the Panel of Chairmen of the Constituent Assembly.
Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was born in Nellore district.
Ambedkar proposed Hyderabad as India's second capital in Thoughts on Linguistic States (1955).
The Statue of Social Justice is at Vijayawada (2024).

items.title: For Mains — Ambedkar & the Making of the Constitution
items.body:
This topic feeds **Mains Paper-II** (clause M2-4b: 'Self-Respect Movement, Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar; Gandhi, Bose, Patel; Ambedkar'). Mains does not want date-recall; it wants you to **assess Ambedkar's dual legacy** — as a social reformer and as the chief architect of constitutional social justice — and to analyse how the Constituent Assembly built a durable democracy.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes/context | Graded caste inequality; failure of pure social reform; colonial constitutional reforms opening political space |
| Methods | Satyagraha (Mahad, Kalaram), press (Mooknayak), parties (ILP, SCF), constitutionalism (Round Table, Poona Pact) |
| Contribution to the Constitution | Chaired Drafting Committee; defended strong Union + federal balance; 'constitutional morality'; safeguards for weaker sections |
| Significance | Converted untouchability from a charity issue into a rights-and-representation issue; embedded social justice (reservation, Art 17) |
| Criticism/limits | Tension with Gandhi over separate electorates; resigned 1951 over the stalled Hindu Code Bill; limits of legal equality without social change |
| Way forward | Realising 'constitutional morality' and substantive (not merely formal) equality |

**Data points / quotes to deploy:** Poona Pact (1932) raised reserved provincial seats from 71 to 148; Drafting Committee of 7 formed 29 Aug 1947; Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; *Annihilation of Caste* (1936); Ambedkar's warning in his final Assembly speech that political democracy without social and economic democracy is unstable; Article 17 (abolition of untouchability).

**AP angle:** Telugu jurist **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** sat on the Drafting Committee; **Durgabai Deshmukh** (Andhra Mahila Sabha) and **T. Prakasam** shaped the debates — a natural line for an AP-flavoured answer.

**Use in answers:** open with Ambedkar's 'division of labourers' critique; use a two-part body (reformer -> framer); quote his 'constitutional morality' idea; close with the gap between formal and substantive equality. A simple timeline diagram (1927 Mahad -> 1932 Poona Pact -> 1947 Drafting Committee -> 1950 Constitution) strengthens the answer.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-II clause M2-4b (reformers; Gandhi/Bose/Patel; Ambedkar).
Frame his dual legacy: social reformer AND chief constitutional architect.
Quote Poona Pact (71->148 seats), Annihilation of Caste (1936), Article 17, 'constitutional morality'.
Criticism: Gandhi tension, 1951 Hindu Code Bill resignation, formal vs substantive equality.
AP angle: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, Durgabai Deshmukh, T. Prakasam in the Assembly.
